item_name: Irene Glendinning (Coventry University) and IPPHEAE Project — EU-wide Academic Integrity Policy Study
key_findings: The IPPHEAE project revealed significant inconsistencies in how academic integrity policies are implemented across 27 EU member states. Over 5,000 survey responses from students, teachers, and senior managers showed that: (1) Only 35% of teachers believed their institutions had effective plagiarism policies; (2) Inconsistencies exist both within institutions and between countries; (3) Some EU countries (UK, Sweden, Austria, Republic of Ireland, Slovakia) have taken more significant steps to address academic integrity threats; (4) Digital plagiarism detection tools and open communication about academic standards are essential deterrents; (5) Monitoring and reporting of academic misconduct are inconsistent across institutions.
methodology: Mixed-methods comparative study using online questionnaires as the main research instrument. Survey-based design with analysis of almost 5,000 responses covering multiple stakeholder perspectives (students, academic teachers, senior managers). Multi-country comparative analysis across 27 EU member states, with additional qualitative insights from national and international experts. Development of Academic Integrity Maturity Model (AIMM) based on nine criteria: research, training, knowledge level, communications, prevention strategies, use of software, and others.
sample_size: Almost 5,000 survey responses from students, teachers, and senior managers across 27 EU member states; data also derived from national reports for each country studied
geographic_scope: All 27 European Union (EU) member states; core research teams from UK (Coventry University), Poland, Lithuania, Cyprus, and Czech Republic
publication_details: Multiple peer-reviewed publications. Key publications include: (1) Glendinning, I., Orim, S.M. (2022). 'Comparison of Institutional Strategies for Academic Integrity in Europe and Eurasia.' In: Academic Integrity: Broadening Practices, Technologies, and the Role of Students. DOI: 10.1007/978-3-031-16976-2_3; (2) Glendinning, I., Eaton, S.E. (2023). 'Understanding and addressing drivers of corruption in academic publishing.' Handbook of Academic Integrity, 2nd Edition, Springer. DOI: 10.1007/978-981-287-079-7_146-1; (3) Glendinning, I. (2024). 'Looking through the Assurance Lens: Institutional Governance of Academic Integrity Strategies.' Journal of Scholarly Publishing, 56(2). DOI: 10.3138/jsp-2024-1119; (4) Impact of Policies for Plagiarism in Higher Education Across Europe: Results of the Project (2015, Acta Universitatis Matthiae Belii).
replication_status: The IPPHEAE methodology has been replicated and extended. Glendinning co-authored a follow-up Council of Europe-commissioned study on contract cheating across six South East European countries (2017). The research framework and Academic Integrity Maturity Model have been adopted in subsequent studies beyond the original 27 EU countries. ENAI (European Network for Academic Integrity) has adopted the guidelines and frameworks developed from IPPHEAE research.
methodological_limitations: Focus limited to bachelor and master's degree levels, excluding doctoral research and higher. Online questionnaire format may introduce response bias or exclude academics with lower digital literacy. Anticipated high volume of data across multiple languages may have introduced translation or interpretation challenges. Self-reported data from teachers, students, and managers may not reflect actual institutional practices. Snapshot in time (2010-2013); policies have evolved significantly since completion. [uncertain: specific non-response rates, sampling methodology details for different countries]
generalizability: Findings are highly generalizable to European higher education contexts, with specific applicability to EU member states. The study's scope of 27 EU countries and multiple institutional types strengthens generalizability within Europe. Applicability to Vietnamese higher education is moderate: while policy inconsistencies and staff knowledge gaps are likely universal issues, specific policy frameworks, detection methods, and enforcement mechanisms differ significantly between EU and Vietnamese contexts. The AIMM framework could be adapted for Vietnamese HE, but requires localization for Vietnamese educational policy and institutional cultures. The finding that digital tools and communication are essential is universally applicable.
which_debate_claim_it_supports_or_challe: This evidence directly supports claims about: (1) The need for robust institutional policies on academic integrity (including AI-related misconduct); (2) The importance of consistency in policy implementation across institutions; (3) The role of detection tools and transparent communication in deterring academic dishonesty; (4) The widespread lack of effective detection and enforcement systems (only 35% of teachers report effective plagiarism policies); (5) The need for staff development and institutional commitment to academic integrity. It challenges claims that current systems are adequate and suggests that ad-hoc or inconsistent approaches fail to deter misconduct. Indirectly challenges assumptions that students inherently understand academic integrity standards without explicit institutional communication.
policy_implications: Key policy recommendations from IPPHEAE work: (1) Develop and implement explicit, institution-wide academic integrity policies with clear definitions and consequences; (2) Invest in staff training and development on academic integrity issues and detection methods; (3) Deploy digital plagiarism detection software as part of a comprehensive approach (not as sole solution); (4) Establish consistent monitoring and reporting procedures across all departments; (5) Foster transparent communication about academic standards and expectations with students; (6) Align academic quality assurance with academic integrity objectives; (7) Extend academic integrity policies to address emerging forms of misconduct (including contract cheating and, by extension, AI-generated content). For Vietnamese HE: prioritize national-level guidance and QA frameworks similar to UK model; strengthen institutional-level policy implementation and staff knowledge.
how_it_changes_the_analysis: This evidence demonstrates that academic integrity challenges are systemic across Europe and require multi-level policy responses (national, institutional, departmental). The finding that only 35% of teachers report effective policies suggests that current detection and enforcement systems are inadequate, which strengthens the argument for comprehensive AI integrity policies that go beyond detection alone. It shifts the debate from 'whether' policies are needed to 'how' to implement them effectively and consistently. The emphasis on staff training and institutional culture suggests that purely technical solutions (detection tools) are insufficient without supporting change management and staff development. For AI integrity specifically, this implies that policies must address not just detection but also institutional readiness, staff understanding, and student education. The evidence suggests that Vietnamese HE should prioritize building foundational policy infrastructure before addressing emerging AI challenges.
contradictory_findings: [uncertain] Limited explicit contradictory findings in the literature reviewed. However, some studies suggest that higher levels of plagiarism detection do not necessarily lead to reduced misconduct if enforcement is weak or inconsistent. Also, some research indicates that awareness of detection tools may encourage more sophisticated cheating strategies rather than deterring cheating altogether. The 35% effectiveness rating could be interpreted as indicating that 65% of institutions lack effective detection systems, which may overstate or understate actual detection effectiveness depending on teacher perception versus objective metrics.
alternative_interpretations: Alternative interpretation 1: The inconsistencies documented by IPPHEAE may reflect deliberate institutional policy variation reflecting different educational philosophies or student populations, rather than policy failure. Stronger institutions may need less stringent enforcement due to higher student integrity standards. Alternative interpretation 2: The low teacher confidence (35%) in institutional policies may reflect unrealistic expectations about what policies can achieve, rather than actual policy inadequacy. Teachers may be comparing against impossible standards rather than measuring actual misconduct detection. Alternative interpretation 3: Variation in policy implementation across EU countries may be appropriate given different national legal frameworks, educational traditions, and labor market needs, rather than requiring harmonization. Alternative interpretation 4: Student misconduct rates may not correlate strongly with policy strength if detection and enforcement are inconsistent; thus, policy documents alone do not deter misconduct without implementation fidelity.
unresolved_questions: How have European HE institutions' academic integrity policies evolved since the 2013 IPPHEAE completion in response to technological change (AI, contract cheating services)?
What specific policy features (explicit definitions, sanctions, appeals processes, student education) are most effective in reducing misconduct across different national contexts?
How do student demographics (socioeconomic background, first-generation status, language proficiency) correlate with misconduct and policy effectiveness?
What is the relationship between institutional policy strength and actual misconduct detection and sanction rates?
How do institutional cultures and leadership commitment affect implementation of published policies?
To what extent are inconsistencies in policy implementation deliberate (reflecting institutional autonomy) versus unintentional (reflecting resource or knowledge gaps)?
How should academic integrity policies be adapted for emerging forms of misconduct including AI-generated work, contract cheating, and collaborative learning ambiguity?
What level of policy harmonization is optimal across diverse European contexts, and who should drive this (EU, national governments, institutions, professional bodies)?

what_evidence_still_missing: Updated post-2015 comparative data on policy implementation across 27 EU member states (original IPPHEAE data is now over a decade old and policies have likely evolved). Empirical effectiveness data: correlation between specific policy features and actual misconduct detection/sanctions (IPPHEAE measured perceptions, not detection rates). Research on implementation fidelity: how closely do institutions follow their published policies in practice? Longitudinal student outcome data: do stronger academic integrity policies lead to better long-term learning outcomes or professional integrity? Comparative analysis with non-EU countries, including Asian and ASEAN contexts, to assess generalizability beyond Europe. Specific research on institutional barriers to policy implementation (resource constraints, institutional culture, staff resistance). Research on student perspectives and understanding of academic integrity across different educational systems and cultures. Updated guidance on AI integrity and contract cheating integration into existing policy frameworks.
recommended_studies: Replicate IPPHEAE methodology with updated questions addressing AI-generated content, contract cheating, and contemporary misconduct forms across 27+ EU countries (2025+)
Conduct implementation fidelity study: audit actual institutional practices against published policies across representative sample of 100+ European HEIs
Longitudinal study: track cohorts of students in high vs. low policy-strength institutions to measure learning outcomes, integrity development, and post-graduation professional behavior

Cross-regional comparative study: IPPHEAE-style survey across ASEAN, East Asia, and South Asia HEIs to assess applicability and identify cultural/contextual differences in academic integrity attitudes
Mixed-methods study: quantitative survey + qualitative case studies of 10-15 institutions with highest policy maturity (per AIMM) to identify implementation success factors

Effectiveness trial: randomized controlled trial comparing policy intervention (explicit integrity education + detection tool deployment + staff training) vs. control in 20+ institutions, measuring misconduct detection and sanctions

Policy synthesis study: analyze lessons learned from IPPHEAE (2010-2013), subsequent Council of Europe projects, and emerging AI integrity research to develop updated European guidelines and Vietnamese-specific recommendations

Institutional barriers study: qualitative research with policy implementers, academic leaders, and teachers (100-150 interviews across 20+ institutions) to identify implementation obstacles and enablers
feasibility_of_filling_gap: High feasibility for updated comparative survey (IPPHEAE-style): methods are proven, networks exist, estimated cost €500k-1M, timeline 24-36 months. High feasibility for implementation fidelity audit: established auditing methodologies available, cost €250k-500k, timeline 18-24 months. Moderate-to-high feasibility for longitudinal student outcome study: requires institutional partnerships and student tracking (privacy constraints), cost €1M+, timeline 5-7 years (long-term commitment). Moderate feasibility for cross-regional (ASEAN/Asia) comparative study: language and cultural adaptation required, partnerships with regional institutions needed, cost €300k-600k, timeline 24-36 months. High feasibility for case studies and barriers research: qualitative methods are established, access to institutions likely through ENAI/QAA networks, cost €150k-300k, timeline 12-18 months. Moderate feasibility for RCT on policy interventions: requires institutional buy-in, complex randomization logistics, cost €500k-1M+, timeline 24-36 months. Moderate feasibility for policy synthesis and Vietnamese recommendations: literature review + expert consultation, cost €50k-100k, timeline 6-12 months. Overall: feasible to fill major evidence gaps with appropriate funding and institutional partnerships; no insurmountable methodological or logistical barriers identified.
